claim: Singular themself is attested in the standard dialect from the 1970s onwards, but very rarely.
evidence_summary: OED themself, pron. (revised 2013), senses I.2a–b and II.3b: anybody could harm themself (Congregationalist, Boston, 1873); each for themself promises and agrees (memorandum, 1881, Nebraska Supreme Court reports); the person themself (Railway Conductor, 1893); had a finger-bowl to themself (Outlook, 1905); somebody outsmart themself (G. Kanin, 1946); anyone sees themself (P. Nichols, 1967).
finding: Singular themself occurs in edited sources from the late nineteenth century, though several quotations are dialogue or reported speech. The OED adds that themself is often considered nonstandard in later use. The rarity claim is unaffected.
proposed_wording: Examples of the morphologically singular themself are attested from the late nineteenth century, but they are very rare …
inference: When is singular themself first attested in standard written English?

evidence.example: Sense I.2b: 1873 I didn’t know that anybody could harm themself… (Congregationalist); 1946 somebody outsmart themself (Kanin, Born Yesterday). Sense I.2a: 1881 each for themself; 1905 a finger-bowl to themself. Sense II.3b: 1893 the person themself.
evidence.establishes: The first edited attestations precede the 1970s by about a century.
evidence.locator: Meaning & use, senses I.2a, I.2b, II.3b. Accessed 19 November 2026 through the University of Toronto Libraries subscription.
